title: Holy Prabha (Halo for a Buddhist Deity)

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Walter Eisenberg, 1982
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A bronze halo, called a prabha, made to stand behind a figure of a Buddhist deity. It is a metal piece with a tang at the bottom for fitting into a base.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record (title, date, medium, culture, classification, objectName Halo, public-domain flag, image URLs, credit line) and the Met catalog page (period and dimensions)

context: A bronze halo (prabha) from Java, Indonesia, made in the Central Javanese period in the 9th century. It was made to frame a Buddhist deity, and it is about 20.6 cm tall without the tang at the bottom, which would have fitted into a base. The record does not describe its decoration.

descriptions.k: This is a halo made of metal. A halo is a ring of light behind a holy figure. It was made on the island of Java long ago. It once stood behind a statue. What shapes can you find on it?
descriptions.g12: A halo is a glowing shape that frames a holy figure. This metal halo was made on the island of Java, in Indonesia, over a thousand years ago. It stood behind a statue of a Buddhist god. At the bottom is a small peg that fit into a base. What kind of figure do you imagine in front of it?
descriptions.g35: This bronze object is a prabha, a halo that stood behind a statue of a Buddhist deity. It was made on the island of Java in the 9th century and is about 20 centimeters tall. A small peg called a tang at the bottom slid into a base. The statue it framed is missing. How does a halo make a figure look special, even when the figure is not there?
descriptions.g68: A prabha is a halo or aureole made to frame the figure of a deity. This bronze one, from Java in the 9th century, is about 20.6 cm tall and has a tang at the bottom that would have fit into a base. The statue it once framed is not part of the object. Looking at a halo alone invites questions: how does it signal holiness, and what does it tell us about the missing figure and the way it was displayed?
descriptions.g910: This Central Javanese bronze prabha, or halo, was made in the 9th century to surround a Buddhist deity. Its tang shows that it was mounted on a base, and the record describes it as sculpture, not as an ornament alone. Without the figure it framed, the object invites us to consider how a frame can create sacred space and how ritual objects often form sets. How does separating a halo from its figure change what we see, and what do we not know?
descriptions.g1112: Separated from the deity it once framed, this 9th-century Javanese prabha challenges us to read a part as a whole. The Met's record gives its material, date, size, and the tang by which it was mounted, but not its decoration or original ensemble, so we should be cautious about claims regarding use or patronage. The object can still prompt reflection on how halos symbolize radiance and holiness, how Buddhist sculpture was assembled from parts, and how museums display fragments of larger works.

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, classification (Sculpture), objectName (Halo), medium (Bronze), and culture checked against the museum record. The record has no tags and the catalog page has no label text, so descriptions only use the title, dimensions, and the tang. No figures are named, so bare-chested imagery is not a concern, but the decoration is unknown.

teacherNote.context: A 9th-century bronze prabha (halo) from Central Java, about 20.6 cm tall without its mounting tang, made to frame a Buddhist deity. The decoration is not described in the record.
directions: Ask students to sketch the figure they imagine standing in front of the halo, then compare drawings.
Discuss how halos or glowing shapes appear in art from different cultures and what they signal.
Talk about how museums display parts of larger works and what is lost when pieces are separated.
